overview.intro: The Mughal Empire, founded by Babur in 1526, unified most of the subcontinent under one of history's great dynasties. This chapter studies the prescribed sources (the Ain-i-Akbari, Taj Mahal, Jama Masjid and Red Fort), the kings in chronological order, Babur's three battles that consolidated the empire, and Akbar's Rajput policy, steps towards integration, social and educational reforms and the mansabdari system.

blocks.text: Babur, a Chagatai Turk driven from Fergana and Samarkand, turned to India: invited by discontented nobles (Daulat Khan Lodi) and using superior artillery, he defeated Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat (1526) and founded the Mughal Empire. His son Humayun lost it to Sher Shah; Akbar (1556-1605), guided by Bairam Khan at Second Panipat, rebuilt and expanded it, crafting policies of integration - Rajput partnership, religious tolerance (sulh-i-kul), administrative grading (mansabdari) and measured revenue (zabti) - that created the classical Mughal state. The great emperors after him - Jahangir, Shah Jahan, Aurangzeb - extended the empire to its largest extent before decline after 1707.

Sources. Ain-i-Akbari: by Abul Fazl, the third book of the Akbarnama - a detailed gazetteer of Akbar's government: departments, mansabdari grades, revenue statistics, provinces, even recipes and paint formulas - the administrative bible of the reign. Taj Mahal (Agra, built by Shah Jahan for Mumtaz Mahal, 1632-53): the supreme monument of Mughal architecture - white marble, pietra dura, char-bagh garden; a source for the empire's wealth and aesthetics. Jama Masjid (Delhi, 1650-56) and Red Fort (Lal Qila, 1639-48): Shah Jahan's Shahjahanabad; the mosque of sandstone and the fort with Diwan-i-Am and Diwan-i-Khas (the Peacock Throne hall) - sources for urban design, court ceremonial and engineering.

Kings in chronological order. Babur (1526-30): founder; won Panipat, Khanwa, Chanderi; Baburnama. Humayun (1530-40, 1555-56): defeated by Sher Shah at Chausa and Kanauj; exile in Persia; regained Delhi just before death. Akbar (1556-1605): guardian Bairam Khan won Second Panipat (against Hemu); conquests of Malwa, Gondwana, Chittor, Ranthambhor, Gujarat, Bengal, Kabul, Kashmir, Sindh, Baluchistan, Deccan (Ahmadnagar); reforms below; Din-i-Ilahi; Din-i-Ilahi. Jahangir (1605-27): Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri; justice chain-and-bell; Nur Jahan's influence; conquest of Kangra, Mewar (with Khurram); Sir Thomas Roe's embassy. Shah Jahan (1628-58): 'golden age' of architecture - Taj Mahal, Red Fort, Jama Masjid, Peacock Throne; Deccan campaigns; illness sparking succession war. Aurangzeb (1658-1707): empire's greatest extent; Deccan wars against Marathas (Shivaji, then Sambhaji and Rajaram), jizya reimposed (1679), Rajput and Sikh conflicts; long wars strained the empire. After 1707: Bahadur Shah I, Jahandar, Farrukhsiyar, Muhammad Shah ('Rangeela' - Nadir Shah's 1739 invasion), Ahmad Shah, Alamgir II, Shah Alam II (Battle of Buxar 1764; blind emperor), Akbar II, Bahadur Shah Zafar (last emperor, exiled 1858).

Babur's three battles. First Battle of Panipat (21 April 1526): Babur with about 12,000 men defeated Ibrahim Lodi's 100,000/1,000 elephants using tulughma (encircling tactics) and Rumi (Ottoman) artillery behind a line of carts; Ibrahim died on the field; Delhi and Agra fell - foundation of the empire. Battle of Khanwa (1527): against Rana Sanga of Mewar leading a Rajput confederacy; Babur's artillery, discipline and declarations of jihad-ish resolve won; broke Rajput power in the north - consolidating the conquest. Battle of Chanderi (1528): against Medini Rai of Chanderi; the Rajput fortress fell; the garrison fought to the death (jauhar); Malwa opened. (The syllabus's three battles = Panipat, Khanwa, Chanderi; the later battle of the Ghaghra (1529) against the Afghans is sometimes added.)

Akbar - Rajput policy. Akbar replaced confrontation with partnership: matrimonial alliances (e.g., with the Kachhwaha prince Bhagwant Das's family - Jodha Bai/ Harkha Bai married 1562; princesses of Bikaner and Jaisalmer), high mansabs and commands for Rajput chiefs (Man Singh, Bhagwant Das, Todar Mal's colleague network), respect for their customs, and freedom to keep their faith - but no separate kingdoms. Chittor (1567-68) fell after fierce siege (jauhar; massacre); Ranthambhor (1569) followed; Udaipur's Rana Pratap resisted at Haldighati (1576) - a stalemate Mewar remembered as heroism. The policy won the Rajputs as sword-arm and administrators of the empire, integrating them as partners in empire-building rather than subjects.

Akbar - steps towards integration. Akbar sought a state transcending religion: abolition of the jizya (1564) and of the pilgrimage tax; translation bureau (maktab khana) rendering Sanskrit works into Persian; cultural synthesis in painting, music (Tansen), architecture (Fatehpur Sikri's blend of styles); a rationalised calendar and the Ilahi era; the Ibadat Khana (1575) debating all faiths; and in 1582, Din-i-Ilahi - a personal ethical order (few joined, but the principle of sulh-i-kul - peace with all - marked policy). Matrimonial alliances, respect for cow-protection sentiments in court orders, and treatment of Hindu colleagues as partners completed the integration.

Akbar - social and educational reforms. Social: banned sati (unless the woman's free consent), legalised widow remarriage, discouraged child marriage, banned forcible conversions, permitted temple-building, and set example in personal conduct. Educational: made education universal in principle, ordered schools for Hindus and Muslims in every town, taught 'the sciences' alongside scripture, patronised Persian translations and histories (Akbarnama itself), supported the imperial library and atelier of painters, and encouraged debate at the Ibadat Khana. He also reformed the calendar (Ilahi era), standardised weights and measures, and unified the currency.

Akbar - mansabdari system. Akbar graded all nobles and officers into mansabs: zat (personal rank fixing status and salary) and sawar (cavalry rank fixing the number of horsemen to maintain). Ranks from 10 to 10,000+; pay fixed by zat; the mansabdar received cash or a jagir (revenue assignment) and must maintain the quota of cavalry, horses and equipment; review and branding (dagh) and descriptive rolls (chehra) checked the troopers; the system was transferable, non-hereditary, and made the emperor the fountain of all careers. It knit a composite nobility (Turani, Irani, Rajput, Shaikhzada) into one service and is the backbone of Mughal administration.

items: Babur - Founder (1526-30); won Panipat, Khanwa, Chanderi; author of the candid Baburnama.
Humayun - Lost and regained the empire; died 1556; his tomb inspired Taj architecture.
Akbar - The Great: Rajput partnership, sulh-i-kul, mansabdari, zabti revenue, Fatehpur Sikri.
Abul Fazl - Historian of the reign; author of the Akbarnama and Ain-i-Akbari.
Raja Man Singh and Todar Mal - Rajput general and revenue minister who embodied Akbar's partnership policy.
Jahangir, Shah Jahan, Aurangzeb - Successors: justice chain-and-bell; architectural golden age; empire's greatest extent and overextension.
Lodi decline and Babur's superior artillery and tactics.
Sher Shah's brief but brilliant administration (rupees, sarais, GT road) as a base to build on.
Akbar's policy of integration winning Rajput and other partners.
Mansabdari and zabti revenue creating a stable, funded empire.
Political unification of most of the subcontinent under one dynasty for two centuries.
Composite administrative culture: Persian bureaucracy, Rajput military partnership, Indian revenue expertise.
Architectural golden age (Taj, Red Fort, Jama Masjid) and court culture (painting, music, literature).
Overextension and religious controversy under Aurangzeb beginning 18th-century decline.

blocks.text: Zat vs Sawar: Personal rank fixing status/salary versus cavalry rank fixing troops to be maintained.
Sulh-i-kul vs Din-i-Ilahi: Akbar's policy principle of peace with all versus his personal ethical order with few followers.
Panipat (1526) vs Khanwa (1527): Victory over Ibrahim Lodi founding the empire versus victory over Rana Sanga consolidating it against the Rajputs.
Iqta vs Jagir: Sultanate revenue assignment for service versus Mughal salary-substitution assignment within mansabdari.

items: Saying Babur won at Khanwa before Panipat - Panipat (1526) came first.
Attributing the Ain-i-Akbari to Akbar or to Todar Mal - it is Abul Fazl's work.
Writing that Din-i-Ilahi was a new religion imposed on all - it was an ethical order with few adherents.
Confusing zat (personal rank) with sawar (cavalry rank).
Saying Akbar abolished sati entirely without the consent clause - the ban allowed a consenting widow's choice; complete abolition came later.
Placing the Taj Mahal under Akbar - it is Shah Jahan's monument.

questions.explanation: The Rajput confederacy's defeat consolidated Babur's conquest.

questions.explanation: Sawar fixed the cavalry quota; zat fixed rank and pay.

questions.explanation: It informed appointments, taxation and court culture.
questions.commonMistake: Translating it as a separate religion.

questions.prompt: Which Mughal emperor built the Taj Mahal, and for whom?
questions.answer: Shah Jahan, in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal (1632-53).
questions.explanation: The pinnacle of Mughal architecture at Agra.
questions.commonMistake: Attributing it to Akbar or Humayun.

questions.prompt: Name Babur's three battles and his opponents in each.
questions.answer: First Battle of Panipat (1526) - against Ibrahim Lodi; Battle of Khanwa (1527) - against Rana Sanga of Mewar; Battle of Chanderi (1528) - against Medini Rai.
questions.commonMistake: Including Ghaghra (1529) as one of the three.

questions.prompt: State any two features of Akbar's Rajput policy.
questions.answer: Any two of: matrimonial alliances with Rajput ruling houses (e.g., Kachhwahas of Amber); high mansabs and commands for Rajput chiefs (Man Singh, Bhagwant Das); respect for their customs and freedom of worship; partnership in administration and conquest; though Chittor and Ranthambhor were stormed when refused submission.
questions.commonMistake: Saying he abolished their kingdoms outright - the policy was partnership.

questions.prompt: Mention any two social reforms of Akbar.
questions.answer: Any two of: banning sati except with the widow's free consent; legalising widow remarriage; discouraging child marriage; banning forcible conversion; permitting temple-building; regulated sale of liquor with licensing.
questions.commonMistake: Claiming sati was abolished without the consent clause.

questions.prompt: Give reasons: Akbar abolished the jizya in 1564.
questions.answer: The jizya - a tax on non-Muslims - marked their inferior status; abolishing it signalled equality of all subjects and fitted Akbar's policy of sulh-i-kul. It won the goodwill of his Hindu majority, especially the Rajputs whose partnership he sought, and unified the empire ideologically. Together with ending the pilgrimage tax (1563), it made citizenship, not creed, the basis of the state.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between the zat and sawar ranks of the mansabdari system.
questions.answer: Zat was the personal rank: it fixed the mansabdar's status in court and his personal salary (and the pay of his troopers when paid from the centre). Sawar was the conditional cavalry rank: it fixed the number of horsemen he had to maintain when on duty, verified at reviews with branding (dagh) and descriptive rolls (chehra). A high zat with low sawar was common for administrators; equal or high sawar indicated active field command. The two together graded the entire Mughal nobility.
questions.explanation: Define each, then relate the two.
questions.commonMistake: Treating them as identical double ranks.

questions.prompt: Explain Akbar's steps towards integration of diverse communities into one empire.
questions.answer: Religious: abolition of the pilgrimage tax (1563) and jizya (1564); the Ibadat Khana (1575) at Fatehpur Sikri where scholars of all faiths debated; sulh-i-kul as state principle; the Din-i-Ilahi (1582), a personal ethical order (few followers but a symbolic synthesis); respect for Hindu sentiments in court orders. Political: the Rajput policy of marriage alliances, high mansabs and shared command, making Rajputs partners rather than subjects; fair treatment of other groups. Cultural: the maktab khana translation bureau rendering Sanskrit classics (Mahabharata as Razmnama, Ramayana) into Persian; synthesis in painting, music (Tansen) and architecture (Fatehpur Sikri's blended style). Administrative: uniform mansabdari for all communities, merit-based promotion, and Todar Mal's revenue settlement applied equally. Social: reform of sati, widow remarriage, and bans on forcible conversion. Together these steps made the empire a composite state whose legitimacy rested on participation, not creed.
questions.explanation: Religious + political + cultural + administrative + social steps.
